title: Knowing Your Strength
note: A ruler who has settled on punishment among the means measures the four kinds of strength.

couplets.plain: Weigh the strength of the task, your own strength, your enemy’s strength and the strength of allies, then act.
couplets.pm: Weigh the strength of the work you plan, your own strength to finish it, the strength of the enemy who will try to stop it, and the strength of allies on both sides, and act if yours is greater. The work’s strength is judged by what it involves, such as besieging a fort. If you are weaker, defeat is certain. If you are equal, victory is in doubt. Drop it in both cases.

links.quote: Weigh the strength of the task, your own strength

couplets.plain: For those who know what they can do, know what must be known, and stay fixed on it as they go, nothing is out of reach.
couplets.pm: Rulers who know what task they can manage and what strength it calls for, and who march on the enemy with mind, word and body fixed on it, find nothing impossible. They obtain everything. What they can do covers the task, themselves and the enemy, so what must be known is the strength of allies.

links.remove: The ruler and the campaign are his reading and the old English’s. The Tamil says only those who go on.

couplets.plain: Many, not knowing the strength they have, set out on a surge of zeal and broke halfway.
couplets.pm: Many rulers in the world, not knowing the measure of their own strength, began in a rush of spirit to act against those stronger than them, were pressed hard and fell halfway with the work undone. Those with wisdom, the best of the three powers, are few, which is why he says many. So begin only when you know your strength.

links.quote: not knowing the strength they have

couplets.plain: Those who won’t live at peace, don’t know their measure and admire themselves are quickly ruined.
couplets.pm: A ruler who neither lives in accord with neighbouring rulers nor knows the measure of his strength, but admires himself and makes enemies of them, is quickly ruined. There are only two courses with neighbours: be friends, or make an enemy knowing your strength. One who does neither and takes them on while weak never has a firm place.

couplets.plain: Even a cart loaded with peacock feathers will break its axle, if you pile them too high.
couplets.pm: Even a cart carrying peacock feathers will break its axle if they are loaded beyond what it can bear. “Even” marks both the cart’s strength and the feathers’ lightness. It says something else by this: a ruler who makes enemies of many because each is weak loses his strength, strong as he is, when they unite. So don’t make enemies of many who may join together.

links.quote: if you pile them too high
a cart loaded with peacock feathers will break its axle
links.reason: A cart’s axle gives way under a mass of peacock feathers.

links.quote: will break its axle, if you pile them too high

couplets.plain: Those who have climbed to the tip of a branch and try to go further will lose their life.
couplets.pm: People who have climbed to the end of a branch and, in their zeal, strive to climb beyond it will find that zeal the end of their life. It says something else by this: a ruler who has marched on his enemy as far as he can, and then pushes on in a surge of spirit, will end not the work but his own life. Know the limit and stop there.

couplets.plain: Give in the right way, knowing your limit. That is how to look after your wealth as you spend it.
couplets.pm: Give in the proper way, knowing the limit of your wealth, because that is how to live while taking care of it. Split what you have into four: spend two parts on yourself, keep one against trouble, and give one. Taking care means making wealth, which is no one’s friend, a friend to you. If spending stays below income, wealth never leaves.

links.quote: Give in the right way, knowing your limit

couplets.plain: The way in may be narrow, but there is no harm, as long as the way out is no wider.
couplets.pm: Even if the path by which wealth comes to rulers is small, no harm comes of it, as long as the path by which it goes is no larger. Income and spending may even be equal, and there is still no harm.

links.quote: as long as the way out is no wider

links.remove: The tank and its channels are the old English’s image. The Tamil says only the way in and the way out.

links.quote: the way out is no wider

couplets.plain: A life not lived within its limit seems to be there, then is not, then vanishes without a trace.
couplets.pm: The life of someone who can’t live within the limit of their wealth seems to exist but in truth does not, and later even the appearance goes. Living within the limit means giving and enjoying no more than you have. At first the ruin doesn’t show, which is why it seems to be there. This is the harm of spending more than your income.

links.quote: A life not lived within its limit

couplets.plain: Helping others without weighing what you have will quickly destroy your wealth.
couplets.pm: Helping others in a way that doesn’t weigh how much you have quickly destroys the extent of your wealth. Even helping others must not go too far. These last four couplets single out the strength of wealth, a part of greatness among the three powers, because it matters so much.

links.reason: Helping others without weighing what you have soon ruins your wealth.
